definition: The part of a spacecraft that helps it land safely on another world. It has a rocket engine and landing legs. On the Apollo missions, the descent stage stayed on the Moon and acted as a launch pad for the top half.
analogy: Think of it as the spacecraft's landing helper!

definition: The top part of the Apollo lunar module. It carried the astronauts off the Moon and back up to their spacecraft in orbit.
analogy: It is like the lift that takes you back up after you have explored the ground floor.

definition: A spacecraft that lands on a planet or moon and stays in one place to do science.
analogy: A lander is like a science station that stays put.

definition: A robot vehicle with wheels that drives around on another world to explore and study rocks.
analogy: A rover is a robot geologist on wheels.

definition: A spacecraft that travels around and around a planet or moon, studying it from above.
analogy: It is like a satellite camera circling the world.

definition: A robotic spacecraft sent to explore space, often flying past planets on a long journey.
analogy: A probe is a robot explorer on a one-way trip.

definition: When a spacecraft zooms past a planet or moon without stopping or landing, taking measurements as it goes.
analogy: Like taking photos from a car window as you drive past a landmark.

definition: A trick where a spacecraft flies close to a planet and uses its gravity to change direction and gain speed, saving fuel.
analogy: Like swinging around a lamppost to change direction quickly.

definition: A panel of special mirrors that bounces light straight back to where it came from. Scientists fire lasers at the ones on the Moon to measure its distance very precisely.
analogy: Like a bicycle reflector that shines back at a car's headlights.

definition: An instrument that feels tiny shakes in the ground, like earthquakes, moonquakes or marsquakes.
analogy: It is like a doctor's stethoscope listening to a planet's heartbeat.

definition: A shaking of the ground on Mars (or the Moon). The waves travel through the inside of the world and help scientists learn what is deep inside.
analogy: Like tapping a melon and listening to work out what is inside.

definition: An instrument that splits light or other energy into its parts to work out what something is made of. Each chemical element leaves its own pattern.
analogy: Every element has its own colour fingerprint, and a spectrometer reads it.

definition: An instrument that gently zaps a rock with tiny particles and X-rays, then measures what bounces back to find out which elements the rock contains.
analogy: Like knocking on a door and working out who is home from the answer.

definition: A power source that turns heat from slowly decaying radioactive material into electricity. Spacecraft far from the Sun, like Voyager, use them because sunlight is too weak there. Their power drops a little every year.
analogy: Like a very long-lasting battery that runs on heat.

definition: A panel that turns sunlight into electricity. On Mars, dust can cover solar panels and reduce their power.
analogy: Like a leaf catching sunlight to make energy.

definition: The giant bubble that the Sun's wind blows around our solar system. Its outer edge is called the heliopause. Beyond it is interstellar space.
analogy: Like the bubble around a boat moving through water.

definition: The space between the stars, beyond the Sun's bubble of solar wind. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are the only working spacecraft there.
analogy: Leaving our Sun's 'neighbourhood' and entering the space between neighbourhoods.

definition: NASA's set of giant radio dishes in California, Spain and Australia. Because they are spread around the world, at least one can always talk to faraway spacecraft as Earth turns.
analogy: Like three friends taking turns to keep a phone call going.

definition: A day on Mars. It is about 24 hours and 40 minutes long, a little longer than a day on Earth.
analogy: Mars days are just a bit longer than ours, so the team's schedule slowly shifts.

definition: The loose dust, soil and broken rock that covers the Moon and other worlds.
analogy: Like a layer of powdery sand mixed with gravel.

definition: An iron mineral that often forms in water. Opportunity found small balls of hematite on Mars, nicknamed 'blueberries'.
analogy: A clue left behind by water, like a ring left in a bathtub.

definition: A bowl-shaped hole made when a space rock smashes into a planet or moon.
analogy: Like the hole a pebble makes when you drop it into flour.

definition: A large, dark, flat plain on the Moon made of ancient lava. Early astronomers thought they were seas, so they are called 'mare', Latin for sea.
analogy: Giant frozen lakes of rock.

definition: A way to land on Mars by wrapping the lander in big airbags so it can bounce and roll to a stop. Mars Pathfinder, Spirit and Opportunity landed this way.
analogy: Like wrapping a present in bubble wrap before dropping it.

definition: The special six-wheel suspension used by NASA Mars rovers. It lets the wheels climb over rocks while keeping the rover steady.
analogy: Like a seesaw on each side that keeps all six wheels touching the ground.

definition: A gold-plated record carried by Voyager 1 and 2 with pictures, music, greetings and sounds from Earth, in case anyone ever finds the spacecraft.
analogy: A message in a bottle thrown into the ocean of space.

definition: The data a spacecraft sends back to Earth about its health and its science measurements.
analogy: Like a spacecraft sending home a report card.

definition: A spacecraft or part of one that is crashed into a world on purpose, so scientists can study what it throws up.
analogy: Like throwing a stone into a puddle to see what splashes out.

definition: A huge ring of icy objects beyond Neptune. Pluto and Arrokoth are in the Kuiper Belt.
analogy: Like the solar system's freezer full of leftovers from when the planets formed.
